newsitem.title: TURKEY: Israel's Levy meets Turk leader after Erbakan rap.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Levy meets Turk leader after Erbakan rap.

text.p: Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy met Turkey's main opposition leader on Wednesday with a pro-Palestinian reprimand from the country's first Islamist prime minister still ringing in his ears.

Levy had breakfast with Motherland Party (ANAP) head Mesut Yilmaz at a five-star hotel in the capital before paying a visit to the mausoleum of modern Turkey's secularist founder Kemal Ataturk, Anatolian news agency said.
He later met with members of parliament's foreign affairs committee before a planned flight to Istanbul for talks with Turkish business leaders later in the day.

Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan told Levy in no uncertain terms on Tuesday that improved relations depended on Israel giving up its claim to the whole of Jerusalem and handing occupied land over to the Palestinians.
"It is natural, as with all other countries, that developing our relations with Israel is part of our programme," he told reporters with Levy sitting by his side.

"In this connection, Israel also has large responsibilities. ...Above all it must always recognise that Jerusalem is a sacred city for all peoples...for Moslems as well as for Christians and Jews," Erbakan said.

He said Israel must also halt construction of new Jewish settlements in and around Jerusalem and withdraw from the occupied lands, in line with U.N. resolutions. Israel says Jerusalem is its eternal and united capital.
"Levy's face dropped while Erbakan spoke," the liberal Yeni Yuzyil daily said in description of the meeting.

Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller had earlier stressed positive developments in trade and cooperation links. On Wednesday, the foreign ministry said there was no contradiction between her views and the criticism made by Erbakan.

"The comments by both the prime minister and the deputy prime minister (Ciller) reflect traditional Turkish foreign policy. There were nothing new in it," foreign ministry spokesman Omer Akbel told a news briefing.
Turkey was one of the first Moslem states to recognise Israel but has always expressed support for the Palestinians.
Levy struck a more optimistic note than Erbakan.
"Another step has been taken in relations between the two countries," he said. "I believe in the future these relations will develop further."

Levy made clear he hoped to smooth relations with Erbakan and his Islam-based Welfare Party in a bid for political ties more in line with the warm military relations and growing commercial links the two countries already enjoy.

The meeting between the two, which lasted for 45 minutes, ended days of speculation over whether Erbakan -- who campaigned against Turkish military ties to Israel -- would receive Levy at all. Erbakan finally agreed on Monday to see the Israeli envoy.
